knowledge_point.title: Integrating Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments

question.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=24 x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=24\,\Longrightarrow\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{24}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{48}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{48}}9 \sin{\left(24 x \right)}\,\text{d}x &= {\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}9\sin(u)\cdot \frac{1}{24}\,\text{d}u \\ &= \frac{3}{8}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sin(u)\,\text{d}u \\ &= - \frac{3 \cos{\left(u \right)}}{8}\big|_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= 0-(- \frac{3}{8}) \\ &= \frac{3}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

If we let $u=10 x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=10\,\Longrightarrow\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{10}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{20}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{20}}9 \sin{\left(10 x \right)}\,\text{d}x &= {\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}9\sin(u)\cdot \frac{1}{10}\,\text{d}u \\ &= \frac{9}{10}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sin(u)\,\text{d}u \\ &= - \frac{9 \cos{\left(u \right)}}{10}\big|_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= 0-(- \frac{9}{10}) \\ &= \frac{9}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=9 x + \frac{\pi}{3},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=9\,\Longrightarrow\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{9}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{27}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\pi}{3}$ | $\frac{2 \pi}{3}$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{27}}\sin{\left(9 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}\,\text{d}x &= {\int }_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}}1\sin(u)\cdot \frac{1}{9}\,\text{d}u \\ &= \frac{1}{9}{\int }_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}}\sin(u)\,\text{d}u \\ &= - \frac{\cos{\left(u \right)}}{9}\big|_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}} \\ &= \frac{1}{18}-(- \frac{1}{18}) \\ &= \frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=2 \pi x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2 \pi\,\Longrightarrow\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2 \pi}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{1}{4}}\cos{\left(2 \pi x \right)}\,\text{d}x &= {\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}1\cos(u)\cdot \frac{1}{2 \pi}\,\text{d}u \\ &= \frac{1}{2 \pi}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\cos(u)\,\text{d}u \\ &= \frac{\sin{\left(u \right)}}{2 \pi}\big|_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= \frac{1}{2 \pi}-(0) \\ &= \frac{1}{2 \pi}\end{aligned}
$$
